individual_reviews.label: reviewer_1

review.Summary: The paper presents StyleAR, the first multimodal autoregressive (AR) model approach for style-aligned text-to-image generation. It avoids the requirement of text-image-to-image triplet data by converting the problem into binary text-image training: stylized images are generated using a diffusion model (InstantStyle), but the reference style image is omitted from supervision. The model uses a frozen CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler to produce style tokens, injects Gaussian noise, and applies a SAM-based style-enhanced token mechanism at inference to reduce content leakage. Training mixes raw and stylized images in a 1:3 ratio, and DPO post-training improves prompt adherence. Experiments compare against diffusion-based baselines, showing competitive prompt adherence and style consistency, with ablations validating each component.
Strengths: The paper introduces a novel and elegant solution to the triplet-data bottleneck in AR-based style-aligned generation, converting it to binary data training by dropping the reference style image from supervision.
The style-enhanced tokens technique effectively suppresses content leakage, as demonstrated by the ablation and qualitative results.
The mixed raw/stylized training data strategy (1:3 ratio) is well motivated and validated through ablation experiments.
Evaluation includes multiple metrics (CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO) and a user study, comparing favorably against a diverse set of diffusion baselines.
The method integrates additional structural conditions (e.g., depth maps), showing potential for broader controllable generation.
Weaknesses: Comparison is limited to diffusion-based baselines; no direct comparison with existing AR-based style/personalization methods is provided, weakening the claim of being the first and best AR approach.
The evaluation scale is quite small (10 style images, 20 prompts, 800 generated images), and no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are reported for the automatic metrics.

Despite being an AR method, the training data is still generated by a diffusion model (InstantStyle); the style diversity is limited to 80 hand-picked styles and is bounded by InstantStyle's capability, which may limit generalization.
Key hyperparameters such as the residual ratio alpha in Eq. (2), Gaussian noise strength gamma, and the number of style tokens (M=16) are not ablated or justified.
The DPO post-training details are sparse: the VLM used for ranking is not named, and it is unclear whether ranking accounts for style consistency or only semantic alignment.
No code or dataset is released, and some experimental details (raw dataset exact composition, compute budget) are omitted, hampering reproducibility.
Questions: How many participants were involved in the user study, and what exact questions/scales were used to evaluate prompt adherence and style consistency?
What specific values of alpha and gamma were used in Eq. (2), and how sensitive is performance to these hyperparameters?
Does the method require SAM segmentation on the reference image at every inference, and what is the computational overhead or failure rate for abstract or non-photographic styles?
Why were AR-based style transfer or personalization methods (e.g., [31], [44]) not included in the comparison, and how would the results change if compared to a fine-tuned AR text-to-image model?
Which VLM was used for DPO ranking, and how exactly were chosen/rejected pairs constructed to ensure they capture style consistency rather than just semantic alignment?
Limitations: The method still relies on a diffusion model to generate stylized training data, meaning the style space is inherently constrained by that generator and the 80 chosen artistic styles.
The evaluation suite is small and may not represent the diversity of real-world styles and prompts, limiting the conclusiveness of the reported gains.
The SAM-based style-enhanced tokens add an extra inference-time segmentation step, which may be expensive or unreliable for certain style images.
No code, data, or trained models are released, making the work difficult to reproduce and build upon.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, such as unauthorized imitation of copyrighted artistic styles or artwork.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_2

review.Summary: The paper proposes StyleAR, an autoregressive (AR) multimodal model for style-aligned text-to-image generation. To avoid costly text-image-to-image triplet data, it uses a data curation pipeline that synthesizes stylized images with a diffusion model and retains only prompt-stylized-image binary pairs, mixing them with raw image-text data. The model uses a frozen CLIP encoder and a perceiver resampler to inject style tokens, and introduces style-enhanced tokens based on Gaussian noise injection and SAM-based feature subtraction to mitigate content leakage. DPO post-training is applied to improve prompt adherence. Experiments compare with diffusion baselines using CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO, and a user study, and report competitive performance.
Strengths: The paper addresses an underexplored setting: style-aligned generation with autoregressive models, and proposes a binary-data training strategy that avoids the need for large triplet datasets.
The data curation idea of mixing stylized and raw image-text data is simple and appears effective in ablations, improving style consistency without hurting prompt adherence.
The style-enhanced token mechanism combining Gaussian noise injection and SAM-based feature subtraction is a novel approach to reduce content leakage.
The integration of DPO post-training and additional structural conditioning demonstrates the flexibility of the proposed framework.
The paper includes both quantitative metrics and a user study, and reports competitive qualitative results against several diffusion-based baselines.
Weaknesses: The method does not achieve state-of-the-art performance on any reported metric; the claimed 'superior balance' is subjective, and the high CLIP-I/DINO of IP-Adapter is attributed to content leakage without a direct quantitative measurement of leakage.
Comparisons may be unfair because StyleAR is based on Lumina-mGPT (a much larger AR model) while baselines use SDXL or SD1.5; model sizes, compute, and inference costs are not reported.

There is a train/inference mismatch: training injects Gaussian noise into CLIP features, while inference uses SAM-subtracted residual features; no ablation or justification is provided for this discrepancy.
Key design choices are not ablated: perceiver resampler, number of style tokens, noise strength gamma, residual ratio alpha, DPO ranking details, and LoRA rank.
The paper lacks reproducibility details: no code, no full architecture specifications, incomplete dataset descriptions, and many references and figures are redacted or contain typos/duplicated text.
The evaluation is limited to 10 styles, 20 prompts, and 800 generated images, with no statistical significance tests and insufficient detail on the user study setup.

Although the data curation avoids triplet data, it still depends on a diffusion model (InstantStyle) to generate stylized images, which may inherit style biases or quality limitations; this is not analyzed.
Questions: How does the model generalize to unseen reference styles at test time when training is self-supervised on already stylized images without explicit style labels?
What is the effect of gamma (noise strength) and alpha (residual ratio) on prompt adherence and style consistency? Were these tuned?
Why not train with the SAM-based style-enhanced tokens directly, instead of only using them at inference?
How was the DPO preference data constructed and validated? What VLM was used, and how reliable is it for style-alignment preferences?
What are the exact training details: number of steps, optimizer, LoRA application, and total compute? How does StyleAR's parameter count compare to the diffusion baselines?
Can the proposed binary-data method be directly compared with triplet-based instruction tuning using the same AR backbone to quantify the benefit?
How is 'content leakage' quantified beyond qualitative inspection and indirect CLIP-I/DINO changes?
What is the coverage of the 80 styles and 200 prompts, and how does the method perform on styles outside this distribution?
Limitations: The disclosed limitation is that the current implementation requires depth map extraction for content control rather than accepting direct content image input.
Missing limitations include the dependence on a diffusion model for data synthesis, potential style bias in the curated dataset, the small evaluation scale, and the lack of analysis of failure cases.
The paper does not discuss potential negative societal impacts, such as style mimicry, copyright infringement, or misuse for deceptive content generation.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_3

review.Summary: The paper proposes StyleAR, a method for style-aligned text-to-image generation with autoregressive (AR) models using binary text-image data instead of triplet data. It introduces a data curation strategy that synthesizes stylized images via a diffusion model (InstantStyle) but discards the reference style image, creating binary data, and mixes these with raw images for training. The model uses a CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler to obtain style tokens, injects Gaussian noise to reduce content leakage, and at inference employs SAM-based feature subtraction with a residual path (style-enhanced tokens). DPO post-training is also applied. Experiments compare with diffusion-based baselines, showing competitive or superior performance in prompt adherence and style consistency.
Strengths: Addresses an underexplored problem: enabling AR models for style-aligned generation with binary data, avoiding the need for expensive triplet datasets.
The data curation method of mixing stylized and raw images is empirically shown to improve style consistency.
The style-enhanced tokens technique with SAM and Gaussian noise is a novel approach to mitigate content leakage.
The paper includes extensive comparisons with multiple diffusion baselines, including qualitative, quantitative, and user study evaluations.
Weaknesses: The claim of avoiding the diffusion upper bound is questionable because training data is still generated by InstantStyle, which may limit style diversity and quality.
Evaluation is limited: only 10 reference styles and 20 prompts, with no standard benchmark comparison; the metrics (CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO) may not fully capture perceptual quality.
Methodological details are vague: the SAM-based feature subtraction, residual path, Gaussian noise strength, and DPO implementation are not fully specified, hindering reproducibility.
Table 1 shows StyleAR does not achieve the best score on any single metric; the explanation for IP-Adapter's high scores relies on content leakage, but this is not directly verified.
The ablation study lacks qualitative evidence for content leakage in the 'w/o SE tokens' case, and the contribution of each component (noise vs. SAM) is not disentangled.
The writing has grammar and typographical issues (e.g., 'pose-training' for 'post-training', 'we primary focus'), affecting clarity.
Questions: How exactly is SAM utilized at inference? Is the entire reference image segmented into all objects, and how is the segmentation mask combined with the feature subtraction?
How is the residual ratio alpha in Eq. (2) chosen? Is it tuned, and what is its impact?
How is the Gaussian noise strength gamma determined? Is it fixed or learned, and does it vary across styles or prompts?
What were the exact prompts used to generate the stylized dataset with InstantStyle? Are they unrelated or derived from the evaluation prompts?
Why is a 1:3 ratio of stylized to raw images optimal? Was the ratio searched more finely, and why does more raw data lead to content leakage?
How does the method perform on a standard style-aligned benchmark (e.g., WikiArt) with many more styles?
How many users participated in the user study, and what specific questions were asked?
How does StyleAR generalize to unseen styles not present in the training set? Is there any few-shot adaptation capability?
Can the method be applied to other AR backbones besides Lumina-mGPT?
What are the failure modes? Are there cases where style consistency or prompt adherence degrades significantly?
Limitations: The method still depends on a diffusion model for data generation, inheriting its limitations in style diversity and fidelity.
The current implementation requires a depth map for content control, limiting direct content image input integration.
Evaluation is confined to a small set of styles and prompts, lacking broader generalization studies.
Potential negative societal impact: style imitation could lead to art forgery or copyright infringement, which is not discussed.

individual_reviews.label: reviewer_4

review.Summary: The paper proposes StyleAR, an autoregressive (AR) model for style-aligned text-to-image generation. To bypass the scarcity of text-image-to-image triplet data, it introduces a data curation method that synthesizes stylized images with a diffusion model (InstantStyle) and constructs binary text-image pairs by discarding the reference style image. The model integrates a frozen CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler to produce style tokens, and uses Gaussian noise injection plus SAM-based feature subtraction (style-enhanced tokens) to mitigate content leakage. Training mixes raw images with stylized images and incorporates DPO post-training. Experiments compare with diffusion-based methods, showing competitive prompt adherence and style consistency.
Strengths: Addresses an important and practical data scarcity problem for style-aligned generation in AR models by using binary data instead of hard-to-obtain triplet data.
The style-enhanced tokens technique (SAM segmentation and Gaussian noise) is a thoughtful attempt to reduce content leakage from reference style images.
The architecture using a CLIP encoder with a perceiver resampler to inject style tokens into an AR model is a plausible and technically reasonable approach.
User study results suggest strong style consistency compared to several diffusion-based baselines.
Weaknesses: Fundamental train/inference mismatch: during training, style tokens are extracted from the same image the model is trained to predict, while at inference the reference style image is different; this gap is not analyzed or directly addressed.

The claim of state-of-the-art is not supported by the quantitative results: CLIP-T is lower than InstantStyle, and CLIP-I/DINO are lower than IP-Adapter; the explanation about content leakage is plausible but does not correct for metric bias.
Evaluation is very limited: only 10 reference styles and 20 prompts, no standard style-transfer benchmarks, no statistical tests, and insufficient details about user study participants.
No comparison with existing autoregressive style-aligned or personalization methods (e.g., references [31] and [44]), which weakens the novelty claim.

The data curation still relies on a diffusion model (InstantStyle) to generate stylized images, so the style quality and diversity of training data are bounded by that model; the advantage over triplet data is not clearly demonstrated.
The method description lacks key implementation details: perceiver resampler architecture, training objective, and hyperparameter choices (alpha, gamma), making reproduction difficult.
The paper has many typographical and grammatical errors, and the writing is often unclear.
Questions: During training, the style tokens are extracted from the same image that the model is trained to generate. How does this affect the model's ability to separate style from content? Have you compared training with a separate reference style image (triplet data)?
The ablation shows that increasing the raw-image ratio from 1:3 to 1:6 worsens prompt adherence and causes content leakage. Why would more raw images lead to stronger content leakage?
Can you provide quantitative comparisons with existing autoregressive style-transfer or personalization methods, e.g., those based on AR models?
How are the hyperparameters alpha and gamma chosen? Is the method sensitive to them? Are there ablations for these values?
What VLM is used for DPO data ranking, and what prompt or scoring criterion is employed?
CLIP-I and DINO are known to be inflated by content leakage. Do you have a more style-specific metric or a larger-scale user study to validate style consistency?
What is the computational overhead of running SAM on every reference style image during inference?
Limitations: The train/inference gap is a fundamental concern that may cause the model to rely on content features from the reference image, leading to content leakage.
Training data is limited to 80 styles and 16,000 stylized images, which may not cover the diversity of real-world styles.
The paper does not discuss failure cases, such as abstract reference styles or low-resolution images.
The use of SAM at inference adds computational cost and may not work for non-photographic or abstract images.
The paper does not address potential copyright or ethical issues regarding the use of WikiArt and LAION datasets.

review.Summary: The paper presents StyleAR, a method for style-aligned text-to-image generation using multimodal autoregressive (AR) models trained on text-image binary data rather than triplet data. A diffusion-based model (InstantStyle) is used to generate stylized images from prompts, and these are paired with prompts to form binary training data; raw text-image data are mixed in. A CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler converts reference style images into style tokens in the AR token space. Style-enhanced tokens are formed by Gaussian noise injection and SAM-based feature subtraction to reduce content leakage. DPO post-training improves prompt adherence. Experiments compare with diffusion baselines on prompt adherence, style consistency, and user study, with ablations on data ratio, style-enhanced tokens, and DPO.
Strengths: Addresses an underexplored problem: enabling AR models to perform style-aligned text-to-image generation, where prior work is mostly diffusion-based.
Proposes a practical data-curation strategy that uses binary (prompt, stylized image) data instead of expensive triplet data, and demonstrates that mixing raw images improves style consistency.
Style-enhanced tokens using SAM and Gaussian noise to suppress content leakage is a reasonable and effective mechanism, supported by ablations.
Extensive comparison with several diffusion baselines, including quantitative metrics and a user study, shows competitive performance.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to 10 style images and 20 prompts, yielding only 800 generated images; no standard benchmarks or larger-scale evaluation are used, so generalizability is unclear.

The training setup is self-supervised on the target image itself: style tokens are extracted from the same image that the model must reconstruct. The paper does not adequately explain how the model learns to transfer style to arbitrary new content without content leakage, beyond heuristic noise/SAM masking.

Important implementation details are missing: exact training loss, token sequence construction, perceiver resampler architecture and training, LoRA target modules, DPO VLM and hyperparameters, and inference-time parameters alpha and gamma.

The claim that using binary data avoids the upper bound of the diffusion generator is overstated: the stylized images themselves are produced by InstantStyle, so the range and quality of styles are still bounded by that generator.

Quantitative style metrics (CLIP-I, DINO) can be inflated by content leakage; although the authors note this for IP-Adapter, they do not provide leakage-adjusted metrics or a detailed failure analysis for StyleAR.
Ablation results for data ratio show large CLIP-I/DINO increases with more raw data, which they attribute to content leakage, but no quantitative measure of content leakage is reported.

The paper contains several writing/formatting issues, including incomplete references (redacted entries), duplicated words, and a table caption mislabeled as qualitative, which hurts reproducibility and clarity.
Questions: During training, the style tokens are computed from the same image that serves as the prediction target. How does the model avoid simply copying content from the style tokens, and what exactly prevents the Gaussian noise and SAM subtraction from also removing style information?
What is the exact training objective and sequence format? Please specify the loss function, the order of text/style/image tokens, and how the perceiver resampler is trained with the AR model.
How were the 80 style images and 20 prompts selected, and why was the 1:3 stylized-to-raw ratio chosen as optimal beyond the small ablation? Would the optimal ratio change with dataset scale?
What VLM is used for DPO preference labeling, and what are the DPO hyperparameters (beta, epochs)? How much does DPO improve over a simple supervised fine-tuning with more data?
Please provide the values of alpha and gamma used in experiments and analyze their sensitivity.
Limitations: Small-scale evaluation on a limited set of styles and prompts; no standard style-transfer benchmark.
Dependence on a diffusion-based generator for stylized training data, which constrains the style diversity and may inherit biases.
No release of code, data, or trained models mentioned; reproducibility is further limited by redacted references.
The method currently requires depth-map extraction for structural control, limiting direct content-image style transfer.
Potential social impact: style mimicry of living artists or copyrighted works is not discussed.

review.Summary: The paper presents StyleAR, a method for style-aligned text-to-image generation using multimodal autoregressive (AR) models. The key contribution is a data curation strategy that converts the problem from requiring text-image-to-image triplet data to binary text-image training: stylized images are generated by a diffusion model (InstantStyle), but the reference style image is discarded, leaving only prompt-stylized-image pairs. The model uses a frozen CLIP image encoder with a perceiver resampler to produce style tokens, injects Gaussian noise to mitigate content leakage, and at inference applies SAM-based feature subtraction (style-enhanced tokens) to further reduce leakage. Training mixes raw and stylized images in a 1:3 ratio, and DPO post-training is used to improve prompt adherence. Experiments compare against diffusion-based baselines on CLIP-T, CLIP-I, DINO, and a user study, showing competitive performance. Ablations validate the data ratio, style-enhanced tokens, and DPO.
Strengths: Addresses an underexplored problem: enabling autoregressive models for style-aligned generation, which is typically diffusion-based.
The binary-data training strategy avoids the need for costly triplet data, and the mixing of raw and stylized images is empirically shown to improve style consistency.
Style-enhanced tokens using Gaussian noise injection and SAM-based feature subtraction provide a novel and reasonable mechanism to reduce content leakage.
Includes extensive comparisons with several diffusion baselines, with both quantitative metrics and a user study, and shows competitive performance.
The framework is flexible, allowing additional structural conditions (e.g., depth maps) and DPO post-training.
Weaknesses: Evaluation is very limited: only 10 style images, 20 prompts, and 800 generated images, with no standard benchmarks or statistical significance tests.
No direct comparison with existing autoregressive style/personalization methods, weakening the novelty claim of being the first AR approach.

The training data is still generated by a diffusion model (InstantStyle), so the style diversity and quality are inherently bounded by that generator; the claim of avoiding the diffusion upper bound is overstated.

There is a fundamental train/inference mismatch: during training, style tokens are extracted from the same image the model is trained to predict, while at inference they come from a different reference style image; this gap is not analyzed.

Key implementation details are missing: exact training loss, token sequence construction, perceiver resampler training, LoRA target modules, DPO VLM and hyperparameters, and values of alpha and gamma.
CLIP-I and DINO metrics can be inflated by content leakage; the authors argue this for IP-Adapter but do not provide leakage-adjusted metrics for StyleAR.
The paper has numerous writing and formatting issues, including incomplete references, duplicated text, and unclear descriptions, harming reproducibility.
Questions: How does the model generalize to unseen styles not present in the 80-style training set? Is there any few-shot adaptation capability?
What is the exact training objective and sequence format? Please specify the loss, the token order, and how the perceiver resampler is trained jointly with the AR model.

Why not train with the SAM-based style-enhanced tokens directly instead of only using them at inference? What is the impact of Gaussian noise strength gamma and residual ratio alpha, and were they ablated?
Can you provide quantitative comparisons with existing autoregressive style-transfer or personalization methods (e.g., references [31], [44])?
How is 'content leakage' quantified beyond qualitative inspection and indirect CLIP-I/DINO changes?
What VLM was used for DPO preference labeling, and how were chosen/rejected pairs constructed to capture style consistency rather than only semantic alignment?
Limitations: Small-scale evaluation on a limited set of styles and prompts; no standard style-transfer benchmark is used.
Dependence on a diffusion-based generator for stylized training data constrains style diversity and may inherit biases.
The train/inference mismatch may cause the model to rely on content features from the reference image, leading to content leakage.
No code, data, or trained models are released, making the work difficult to reproduce.
Potential negative societal impacts, such as unauthorized imitation of copyrighted artistic styles, are not discussed.
